About: a crystal and its diffraction pattern

Source

Concept
Two views of one object: a crystal you build, and the pattern of spots it diffracts. The spots respond to the cell — but how? Commit a prediction, then drag a and γ and find out.
Serves
Kinematic diffraction, reciprocal-space intuition, and the Bragg/Laue foundations of X-ray crystallography (NCERT solids / JEE).
Inquiry
Predict how spots move as the cell is stretched and sheared, then click any spot and read |G| and d.
Misconception
A common intuition: "The pattern is a magnified photo — a bigger cell spreads the spots." Stretching a tests that guess against the real reciprocal pattern.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealYou commit to how the spots move before dragging a — then watch what they actually do.
Target the misconceptionA predict-before-drag card names the "magnified photo" guess, then stretching a shows the spots move the other way.
An invariant to huntTwo readouts, |G| and d — multiply them at different spots and see what you notice.
Operational, not vibesEvery claim is a number you read off: |G| in nm⁻¹, d in Å.
Fixed scales, honest motionBoth panels keep a fixed scale, so any motion you see is real, not a re-zoom.
The formal layer is optionalThe reciprocal-basis equations live in the ⚛︎ The Physics revision sheet.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two panels, one instrument

Let’s get our bearings. On the left: a crystal built from sides a, b at angle γ — one atom per cell, with one unit cell outlined. On the right: its diffraction pattern, a spot per (h,k). The (1,0) spot is already selected for you.

2 · Predict: stretch the crystal

Time for your first prediction. You’re about to drag a from 4 to 6 Å, spreading the atom columns apart. What do you think the columns of spots will do?

3 · Drag a and watch

Now let’s test it. Slide a up toward its maximum and keep your eyes on the pattern. Which way does the (1,0) spot go — and does the (0,1) spot follow?

4 · The pattern is backwards

So which spot moved, and which held? For the selected spot, |G| shrank, while the other direction held still.

Now try this: click the farthest spot you can find — are its rows the closest or the widest? Then multiply |G| by d at two spots. What do you notice?

Next, drag b — but predict which spot column answers before you move it. And here’s the product you keep meeting: 2π — |G| × d = 2π at every spot.

5 · Predict: tilt the cell

Now let’s tilt things. You’re about to change γ away from 90°, shearing the cell. What’s your call: will the rows of spots lean so they stay parallel to the sides a and b?

6 · Drag γ and watch the angle

Let’s find out. Slide γ to 75° and beyond, and watch the angle between the yellow line and its highlighted rows. Does it ever change?

7 · Perpendicular, always

Here’s the pattern you’ve been uncovering. The spot sits at 90° to its rows for every cell — squeeze rows closer and the spot pushes farther out, with |G| × d fixed at 2π. Spot rows tilt |90°−γ| off the sides, matching them only at γ = 90°.

8 · Reading atoms backwards

Now put it all together. Spot direction ⟂ rows, distance = 2π ÷ spacing — that’s how crystallographers read unit cells backwards, even DNA’s. So here’s a real one: a crystallographer’s plate shows spots twice as far apart vertically as horizontally, leaning 15° off square. What does that tell them about a cell they can never photograph?

Diffraction from a 2D Crystal

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

This sim puts a two-dimensional crystal beside its diffraction pattern. Change the cell on the left and the spots on the right respond, which is how crystallographers get from a pattern to a cell they can never photograph.

What you'll learn

  • How a spot's position on the pattern depends on the cell's sides a, b and angle γ.
  • How each spot is tied to one family of atomic rows in the crystal.
  • Why a diffraction pattern lights up at particular points: the Laue and Bragg conditions.
  • How to work back from distances and angles on a pattern to the cell that made it.
The two panels, schematic. Left: the crystal and its cell. Right: the pattern, one spot per integer pair (h, k).

What's on screen

  • Atoms (amber), one per cell, with one cell outlined. Red is side a, green is side b, and the yellow arc is the angle γ.
  • Spots (cyan) on the right, one for every integer pair (h, k). The white cross is (000), the straight-through beam.
  • Selected spot (yellow): the line from (000) to the spot. Its set of pale lines appears on the crystal too. Click any spot to select it.
  • Readouts: the selected spot's (h, k), its distance |G| from (000) in nm⁻¹, and its row spacing d in Å.
See itStart from the opening cell with spot (1,0) selected. Watch for: the yellow line from the white cross to the spot, and the pale lines on the crystal that belong to that same spot.

03

The pattern is the reciprocal lattice

The spots are not a magnified picture of the atoms. The sim builds them from the real cell with one rule: each reciprocal vector bj has dot product 2π with its own real vector and 0 with the other.

The definition, with a₃ = ẑ out of the plane.

In the plane, for sides a, b and angle γ, this gives:

The two bases the sim builds.

The spot labelled (h, k) sits at the reciprocal-lattice vector below. Its length is measured in nm⁻¹ because the sim keeps the 2π: reciprocal lengths are 2π divided by a crystal length.

Every spot is a reciprocal-lattice vector. (000) is the beam itself, so the sim leaves it out.
Key idea. Spot positions come from inverting lengths in the crystal, not from scaling them.
See itWith (1,0) selected, stretch a from 4 to 6 Å. Watch for: the spot's |G| on the card falling as the spot moves toward the white cross.
04

Every spot points across its rows

A selected spot has a set of rows: parallel lines of atoms, a distance d apart. They run along t = k a₁ − h a₂.

The dot product cancels term by term.

So G is perpendicular to its rows for every a, b and γ, not just for a square cell. How far out the spot sits is fixed by the spacing of those rows:

Cell sheared to γ = 75°, spot (1,1): d = 3.173 Å, |G| = 19.799 nm⁻¹, and the marked angle is 90.00°.

The Invariant readout |G| × d reads 6.283 = 2π at every spot. (|G| is in nm⁻¹ and d in Å, so the sim divides the product by 10.)

See itWith (1,1) selected, shear the cell from γ = 90° to 75°. Watch for: the pale lines on the crystal and the yellow line on the pattern turning together, with the Invariant staying at 6.283.
05

How the cell sets a spot's distance

The length the sim evaluates for every spot it draws.
a b γ

These sliders move the sim too. The spot is the one you last selected.

  • a appears only in terms that carry h, and b only in terms that carry k. A spot with h = 0 does not depend on a.
  • The shear term −2hk cos γ/(ab) is zero at γ = 90° and whenever hk = 0.
  • Away from 90°, a spot on an axis moves outward, since |G| = 2π|h|/(a sin γ) when k = 0. For hk ≠ 0 the sign of hk decides it. At a = b = 4 Å and γ = 75°, (1,1) falls from 22.214 to 19.799 nm⁻¹ while (1,−1) rises to 25.803.
See itStretch a from 2 to 6 Å with (0,1) selected, then with (1,0). Watch for: |G| on the card holding at 15.708 for (0,1) but changing for (1,0).
06

Why spots appear: Laue and Bragg

A beam of wave vector k scatters elastically from every atom, so |k′| = |k| = 2π/λ. Waves from all the cells add in phase only when the change in wave vector is a reciprocal-lattice vector:

The Laue condition.
Left: two cells scatter in phase when (k′ − k)·R is a multiple of 2π. Right: |k′| = |k| puts k′ on a circle, so only a spot on that circle lights up (λ = 1.54 Å, to scale; the sim has no λ).
  • Bragg's law is the same condition. |Δk| = 2|k| sin θ and |G| = 2π/d give 2d sin θ = λ, with θ measured from the rows.
  • A spot such as (2,0) is the second order of the (1,0) rows. The sim draws it with rows at half the spacing.
  • What the sim leaves out: it draws every G equally bright, with no wavelength, beam direction or intensity. A real exposure shows only the G that its λ and orientation reach.
See itSelect (1,0), then (2,0), then (3,0) at the opening cell. Watch for: the selected spot stepping outward while d on the card falls to a half, then a third.
07

Reading a cell from a pattern

Measure |b₁|, |b₂| and the angle between b₁ and b₂ on a pattern, and the cell follows. The angle is the supplement of γ:

The reciprocal cell angle is the supplement of the real one.

The lengths then give a = 2π/(|b₁| sin γ) and b = 2π/(|b₂| sin γ). Each row of spots leans |90° − γ| off the cell side it belongs to, and matches it only at γ = 90°.

A plate with |b₂| = 2|b₁| and rows leaning 15° gives a = 2b and γ = 105°.

On this plate the angle between b₁ and b₂ is 75°, so γ = 105°. With |b₁| = 10.841 nm⁻¹ the lengths give a = 6 Å and b = 3 Å. A lean the other way would mean γ = 75°.

See itSet a = 6 Å, b = 3 Å, γ = 105° and select (0,1), then (1,0). Watch for: |G| for (0,1) coming out at twice that of (1,0), and the yellow line to (1,0) leaning 15° above horizontal.
08

Where it matters

  • Choosing the radiation. Bragg's law needs λ no larger than 2d. X-rays (Cu Kα: 1.54 Å) suit spacings of a few Å. Visible light at 5000 Å cannot resolve a unit cell.
  • Surfaces. In low-energy electron diffraction (LEED) the spot pattern is the reciprocal lattice of the surface layer, so its spacings give the surface cell directly.
  • DNA, 1952. Franklin and Gosling's Photo 51 was read with the same inversion: its layer-line spacing gave the 34 Å pitch of the helix, and a spot at 3.4 Å gave the rise per base. (A fibre, not a crystal.)
Go deeper: what the sim does not draw
  • Brillouin zone. The same b₁ and b₂ build the Brillouin zone of solid-state physics: the region nearer (000) than to any other spot.
  • One layer. For a single atomic layer only the in-plane part of Δk must equal G. The reciprocal "points" are rods along ẑ, and the sim draws their in-plane lattice.
  • A basis. With two atoms per cell, spots can switch off or dim. With one atom per cell, as here, they cannot.
09

Summary

In one line. Each spot is a reciprocal-lattice vector G: it points at 90° to its rows and sits at 2π divided by their spacing.

Key points

  • The reciprocal basis obeys ai·bj = 2πδij, and spot (h, k) sits at G = h b₁ + k b₂.
  • G ⟂ rows and |G| d = 2π for every a, b and γ.
  • a enters |G| only through terms with h, and b only through terms with k.
  • Spots appear where Δk = G, which is Bragg's law 2d sin θ = λ.

Common mix-ups

  • "The pattern is a magnified photograph of the crystal." It is the reciprocal lattice. Stretching a moves the (1,0) spot toward the centre.
  • "Rows of spots always stay parallel to the cell sides." Only at γ = 90°. Otherwise they lean |90° − γ|, and the angle between b₁ and b₂ is 180° − γ.
  • "Changing a moves every spot." Spots with h = 0 do not depend on a.

Things to try on your own

  • Set γ = 120° and compare the angle between the lines to (1,0) and (0,1) with 180° − γ.
  • Set γ = 75° and compare |G| for (1,1) and (1,−1) with their values at 90°.
  • At γ = 90°, select any spot, double a, and check that |G| × d stays at 6.283.
